title: Seeing Someone Else's Point of View
keyIdea: Your point of view is how things look and feel to you. Other people have their own. To see their side, ask: how would I feel if that happened to me? Then think about what they know, what they want and what has happened to them before. The same moment can feel very different to two people, and seeing both sides helps you choose kind, fair words.

kid: Ben built a big tower. Zara bumped it and it fell. Ben feels sad. Zara feels sorry. It is one moment, but they feel two ways. To see how someone feels, put yourself in their shoes. Ask: how would I feel if that were me?
People only know what they saw. Mia did not see Tom move her cookie. So she looks where she left it, not where it is now.
What has happened before counts too. Sam loves dogs. Kit was knocked over by one, so a big dog scares her.
When you see their side, you can say kind words. Say what they feel. Then find a fair fix.
adult: Perspective-taking means working out what another person feels, thinks and wants from where they stand, not from where you stand. The IB PYP strand for personal, social and physical education asks children of this age to see that others have their own feelings and views. They should use this when they play, read stories and sort out a quarrel.

It has a thinking part and a feeling part. The thinking part is often called theory of mind. It means knowing that people act on what they believe, even when that belief is out of date. The classic test asks where someone will look for a thing that was moved while they were away. The feeling part is empathy: picturing how the moment feels to them. That depends on their past, their likes and their fears.

Common mistakes: thinking everyone feels what you would feel, so a child who loves dogs expects every child to be thrilled by one. Forgetting that the other person did not see what you saw. Calling a feeling wrong instead of asking where it comes from. Jumping to 'on purpose' when the clues point to an accident. A good habit is to name the other person's feeling out loud before you say your own.

In the lab your child gives each child in a story the feeling that fits. They guess where someone will look after missing a change, and sort both sides of a quarrel over a swing. They match three reactions to one dog, then pick the reply that shows they have seen the other side.

familyTip: When you read a story together, pause at a big moment and ask two questions: 'How does this character feel?' and 'Does the other character know what we know?' Then swap: ask your child to guess how you felt about something that happened today.

visual.caption: Does this thought look at the other person's side, or only at mine? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: How would I feel if that were me?
You look upset. Are you OK?
What do you want to do?
I want it, so it is mine.
My way is the only way.
I don't care how you feel.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: give feelings, guess where someone looks, sort both sides, meet one dog and pick the kind reply.

practice.prompt: Lily's balloon floats away into the sky. How might Lily feel?
choices: Nothing, it is only a balloon
practice.hint: Picture it was your balloon. How would you feel?
practice.explain: Lily probably feels sad, because she has lost something she liked. Asking how you would feel helps you guess.

practice.prompt: Omar puts {n} sweets in his bag and goes outside. His sister moves them to a jar. Where will Omar look first?
practice.hint: Did Omar see his sister move the sweets?
practice.explain: Omar looks in his bag. He did not see the {n} sweets being moved, so he still thinks they are where he left them.

practice.prompt: Ruby loves swimming. Finn had a scare in a pool last year. The class goes swimming. Why might they feel differently?
choices: What happened to them before is different
Feelings are always the same for everyone
practice.hint: Think about what each child remembers.
practice.explain: Finn's scare last year makes swimming feel worrying, while Ruby has good memories. Past events shape how people feel now.

practice.prompt: Your friend waited {n} minutes for the computer and you are on it. What shows you see their side?
choices: You waited a long time. I will finish soon.
I was here first, so tough.
practice.hint: Which reply says what your friend feels or did?
practice.explain: Saying 'you waited a long time' shows you have thought about their {n}-minute wait. Then you can offer a fair fix.

pool.prompt: Ava's painting gets rain on it and the colours run. How might Ava feel?
choices: Upset, because her work is spoiled
Bored, because it is just paint
pool.hint: How would you feel if your painting got spoiled?
pool.explain: Ava probably feels upset. She worked on it, and now it is spoiled. Put yourself in her shoes to guess.

pool.prompt: What does 'putting yourself in someone's shoes' mean?
choices: Imagining how things feel to them
pool.hint: It is a saying, not about real shoes.
pool.explain: It means imagining how a situation looks and feels from their side, not yours.

pool.prompt: Zane hides a toy car in a box while Ella is out. Ella left it on the shelf. Where will Ella look first?
pool.hint: What did Ella see last? Did she watch Zane hide it?
pool.explain: Ella looks on the shelf. She did not see Zane move it, so she thinks it is still where she left it.

pool.prompt: Max says 'Oops!' after his ball hits you. What is the best first thought?
choices: I should kick it at him
pool.explain: 'Oops!' is a clue that it was an accident. Checking his side first stops a fight before it starts.

pool.prompt: {n} children want the same book. Which question helps you see the others' side?
choices: Why do you want it today?
pool.hint: Which question asks about their reasons?
pool.explain: Asking why they want it today lets the {n} children share their reasons, and then you can find a fair plan.

pool.prompt: Grandpa jumps when the fireworks go bang. You love fireworks. What is true?
choices: You can each feel a different way
pool.hint: Can two people feel two ways about the same thing?
pool.explain: Two people can feel different ways about the same thing. Loud bangs can startle some people, even if you enjoy them.

pool.prompt: Mo's best friend moved away {n} days ago. Mo is quiet at play time. What could you say?
choices: You must miss your friend. Want to play?
Cheer up, it's not a big deal.
pool.hint: Which reply names how Mo might feel?
pool.explain: Naming the feeling ('you must miss your friend') shows you see Mo's side, then the offer to play helps.
